legend: PDAC with large duct pattern.
Colloid carcinoma of the pancreas also infiltrating the duodenum
Next-generation needle biopsy; ultrathin needles acquire small core tissue fragments, which may demonstrate invasive growth in desmoplastic stroma (cell block).
High-grade adenocarcinoma. Cytology; moderately to poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma demonstrates enlarged, hyperchromatic, crowded, and disordered nuclei (direct smear, Pap staining).

Well-differentiated adenocarcinoma displays nuclei with irregular spacing, anisonucleosis of 4:1, parachromatin clearing, irregular nuclear membranes, and finely vacuolated, lacy-looking cytoplasm (direct smear, Pap staining). This may be difficult to differentiate from the reactive cells of pancreatitis.
Ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic body-tail presenting as a large hypodense mass (arrows) on CT.

Coronal CT of a pancreatic head ductal adenocarcinoma showing the characteristic double duct sign. The arrow indicates the dilated pancreatic duct, and the asterisk indicates the dilated bile duct; the dotted circle indicates the slightly hypodense neoplasm. Inset: The same case shown on MRI / magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography.
Poorly differentiated ductal adenocarcinoma with giant cells.
Moderately differentiated ductal adenocarcinoma within a desmoplastic stroma.
Well-differentiated to moderately differentiated ductal adenocarcinoma.
Moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.
Venous invasion in the peripancreatic fat.
Invasion of a gland into a muscular vessel wall supports the diagnosis of infiltrating ductal adenocarcinoma.
Perineural invasion supports the diagnosis of infiltrating ductal adenocarcinoma.
Poorly differentiated ductal adenocarcinoma.
Well-differentiated, large duct pattern infiltrating haphazardly into fibrotic, atrophic pancreatic stroma.
Adenosquamous subtype.
Hepatoid subtype.
Medullary or lymphoepithelial subtype.
Haphazard glands infiltrating a tissue core.
Challenging case with neoplastic cells wrapped around the edge of desmoplastic stroma.

diagnosis: Estimated age-standardized incidence rates (ASRs, World Standard Population), per 100 000 person-years, of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in 2022.

legend: A Well-differentiated example with foamy gland change.
B Moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.
C Poorly differentiated example with individual pleomorphic cells infiltrating the stroma.
D Large duct pattern.
Poorly defined infiltrating ductal adenocarcinoma obstructing the pancreatic duct with upstream ductal dilation and ductal erythema at the 4 o’clock position. The bile duct is spared.
Poorly defined infiltrating ductal adenocarcinoma subtly narrowing the pancreatic duct. The intrapancreatic bile duct is spared.
Overt features of malignancy are present, including enlarged, crowded, and overlapping hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear membranes, marked anisonucleosis, and variable amounts of cytoplasm.
Foamy gland type adenocarcinoma cells with a deceptively low N:C ratio and abundant, lacy, mucinous cytoplasm, but with irregular nuclear membrane and loss of polarity.
A Axial view of a pancreatic head PDAC showing a hypoenhanced mass (arrow).
B Coronal view showing a dilated bile duct (asterisk) and the pancreatic head tumour (arrow).
A Adenosquamous carcinoma. The squamous component is characterized by eosinophilic cytoplasm and keratin pearl formation, with the glandular component displaying cytoplasmic vacuolation.
B Colloid carcinoma. The neoplastic cells are suspended in pools of stromal mucin.
C Hepatoid carcinoma. The neoplasm is composed of large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
E Signet-ring cell / poorly cohesive carcinoma. Note the individual poorly cohesive cells, some of which contain prominent intracellular mucin.
F Undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclast-like giant cells. The large osteoclast-like cells are non-neoplastic.
D Medullary carcinoma. Note the pushing border, syncytial growth, and associated lymphoid infiltrate.
Significant variation in nuclear size meets the 4:1 rule.
